text.p: Here are highlights of stories reported by Hungary's press, based on information by Nepszabadsag's Hungary Around the Clock service. For further details on how to subscribe to Hungary Around the Clock, please contact Monica Kovacs at (361) 351 2440 or fax your request to (361) 351 7141.
ALL PAPERS

- Young Democrat Tamas Deutsch, chairman of the parliamentary commission probing the Tocsik scandal, said that unidentified persons have continually issued death threats against him and his family. Meanwhile, Marta Tocsik reportedly received letter from a self-styled Justice-Dealing Brigade with the threat that she has only months to live.
- A bomb went off inside a fire extinguisher deposited beside a trash can in downtown Budapest Wednesday evening.
- Negotiations between the government and an IMF delegation began on Wednesday.
- The state's net external debts may vanish within the next two to three years, leaving further debt servicing to the private sector, Vice President of the National Bank said.
- Top executives of the Socialist Party met Premier and party President Gyula Horn to discuss topical issues which may be linked to a special session of the party's presidium convened for today.
- Hungarian Academy of Sciences President Ferenc Glatz said in Parliament that science is the most export-worthy product in Hungarian society today.
- The number of registered unemployed fell by 10,000 in October to 484,500.
- Bids will be invited in a closed two-round tender to sell 25 percent plus one vote in Commercial and Credit Bank.
- The national telecommunications firm Matav has signed a $250 million loan agreement with a banking consortium.
- HUF 100 banknotes will be withdrawn from December 1998.
NEPSZABADSAG
- In an interview with the Vienna Kurier, Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs said the conditions of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Slovakia have made a turn for the worse of late.

- Although Hungary's economic performance has improved considerably in the past two years, excessive bureaucracy still slows development, William Crisp, vice chairman of a conference organised in Budapest by the British weekly The Economist said.
VILAGGAZDASAG
- The cabinet is expected to study a tax fraud report and is to survey monetary policy guidelines for next year.
- Late February may see the next exchange of compensation coupons for shares, this time in the state-owned investment company Dominancia.
MAGYAR HIRLAP

- Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs said in London that Hungary intends to review its economic ties with Yugoslavia, while aiming to involve itself in the reconstruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.
- The social security system will incur a deficit of HUF 13 billion next year, according to the amended draft budget.
- Police spokesman Laszlo Garamvolgyi is leaving his post and will also quit the police force.
- Frigyes Harshegyi, resigned vice president of the National Bank, may join the ranks of the Central European International Bank.

- The 2,760 employees of the electricity company EMASZ are threatening to go on strike with their fellow workers in Essen, Germany, where the minority owner, the consortium RWE-EVS resides, if their wages are not increased by 5.5 percent. Foreign investors put the blame on the government which failed to fulfil its promise to increase energy prices from October 1.
NAPI GAZDASAG
- A new life insurance firm Magyar Elet es Nyugdijbiztosito has received its license to operate.
